summary: The one confirmed in-the-wild hardware-wallet implant (Joe Grand's teardown of a tampered Ledger Nano X, hardwear.io 2026; first sighted Aug 2025) passively sniffed the SPI bus between the Secure Element and the OLED, template-matched rendered glyphs to recover the seed words, and exfiltrated them over an LTE Cat.1 modem — the display was already SE-driven, so an SE-driven screen alone does not stop a passive bus tap, and the implant also spoofed battery telemetry (fixed 10k in place of the NTC, fuel gauge bypassed to read 100%). Ledger's recorded response was procedural (compare against known-good photos, buy from authorised channels, "further hardening for future products"); no vendor in the verified evidence ships a firmware self-test for added bus load, current-sense fingerprinting, or a mechanical no-cavity design. The older, related OLED power side channel (CVE-2019-14353/14354/14356, Reitter 2019; recurrence on the Nano X / S Plus panel in 2023) was closed by every vendor with the same firmware-level idea — make the per-row lit-pixel count independent of the secret (Trezor decoy pixels, Ledger dash-cursor PIN UI, Coldcard right-edge noise) — and Ledger explicitly conceded that physical noise could not hide the data dependency; Coldcard concedes its fix is unproven. The academic tamper-detection literature (ACM TODAES 2026 survey; PDNPulse, IEEE TIFS 2023) shows PDN-impedance fingerprinting can detect board-level implants and even sub-ohm series resistors, but only as an offline VNA bench technique against a golden reference whose limits (manufacturing-flaw confusion, port selection, non-persistent mods out of scope, not tamper-evident) its own authors state; the on-chip "no extra components" runtime variant (eprint 2022/946) failed verification here and remains unestablished. Net: a per-unit self-enrolled baseline taken at first boot cannot catch a supply-chain implant inserted before that boot; the defensible levers today are backup/PIN flows that never render secrets on a sniffable bus, design-derived or fleet (golden-free) electrical fingerprints, and tamper evidence — none of which is yet documented as shipped against this attack class.

findings.claim: A real, field-sold Ledger Nano X implant exfiltrated the 24-word recovery seed by passively monitoring the SPI bus between the Secure Element and the OLED, template-matching rendered a–z glyphs (stored at 0x4D00–0x4E40 in the implant MCU), storing recovered words in flash at 0x7000, and transmitting them over a Luat Air700E 4G LTE Cat.1 modem with an MFF2 eSIM; the implant MCU was an unmarked QFN-20 Cortex-M0+. The tapped bus was already SE-driven, so an SE-driven display by itself does not prevent a passive display-bus tap; it only prevents software on the host MCU from forging the screen.
findings.evidence: Primary slides (Joe Grand, hardwear.io USA 2026, Santa Clara, revised 2026-05-29; 134 MB PDF text-extracted by verifiers) state verbatim: 'OLED connects to the Nano X Secure Element via Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI)', 'Implant monitors SPI traffic between Nano X Secure Element and OLED', 'Template matcher functions look for the glyphs', 'Recovery seed/wallet backup stored in Flash at 0x7000', 'Contents transmitted via cellular module', and the Summary slide 'Monitors the OLED's SPI bus, detects letters used in recovery seed, transmits over 4G LTE'. Sample recovered words shown (GRAPE, SOURCE, VICIOUS, IDEA, EXPECT, SHAFT). Origin: Reddit post ''Nano X' being sold to steal your crypto', August 2025. Slides note 'New iterations of implant have already been spotted' without detail. Grand Idea Studio describes it as a real-world implant discovered inside a Nano X, not a researcher PoC. Caveat: the research question's 'October 2026' and 'CryptoBilis' framing does not appear in this source and needs separate citation.
findings.vote: 3-0 (merged claims 0 and the SE-driven-bus observation from claim 2's verification)

findings.claim: To fit the implant the attackers shrank the battery and deliberately spoofed the device's own power/battery telemetry: a fixed 10 kΩ resistor replaced the pack's NTC thermistor and the fuel-gauge sense resistor was bypassed so the battery always reports 100% full. Any detection scheme that relies on on-device power or battery telemetry must therefore assume the attacker will also tamper with the sensing path.
findings.evidence: Slide 'FRONT-SIDE MODIFICATIONS' reads verbatim: 'Battery has reduced size in order to fit implant / Fixed 10k resistor replaces NTC thermistor from original battery / Fuel gauge resistor bypassed to always appear 100% full'. Independent syndicated coverage of the talk (cryptonews.ru via HTX) repeats the shrunken-battery and fixed-resistor details. Single-sample teardown by one researcher; the 10k value is his measurement/inference.

findings.claim: Ledger's recorded response to the implant was purely procedural — visually check hardware against known-good photos, buy only from Ledger or authorised resellers — with hardening deferred to 'future products'. No shipped firmware-side detection (bus-load self-test, current-sense fingerprint) or mechanical countermeasure is claimed by Ledger, and nothing in Ledger's blog (posts through 2026-10-07) or Donjon security bulletins LSB-021–025 (Jan 2025–Aug 2026) addresses hardware-implant detection; Ledger's SE 'Genuine Check' attests the SE, not the display bus.
findings.evidence: Slide 'LEDGER RESPONSE' lists exactly three items: 'Check hardware integrity against known-good pictures / Follow best practices when buying a device - Directly from Ledger or authorized resellers / Ledger is looking into further hardening for future products'. Verifier checked ledger.com/blog listing (no implant post; the 2026-09-30 'Hardware Wins Over Software' post only says the Secure Screen is SE-driven and 'designed to resist tampering by software') and the donjon LSB index (no bulletin). Confidence is medium because Ledger's response is reported secondhand via the researcher's slide, and WebSearch budget was exhausted so a Ledger press statement could have been missed.

findings.claim: The row-driven SSD1306-class OLED used across 2019-era hardware wallets (Ledger Nano S/X, Trezor One, KeepKey, Coldcard MK1/2, BitBox02 and others) leaks display content into total device power: per-row-cycle current scales with the number of illuminated pixels in that row, which is measurable as voltage across a shunt resistor in the USB power lead with no modification of the wallet, enabling partial recovery of the row layout and, statistically, of the PIN or seed words while they are on screen (CVE-2019-14353 Trezor One, CVE-2019-14354 Nano S/X, CVE-2019-14356 Coldcard; CVE-2019-14355/-14357..-14360, -18673 for other vendors). Both Trezor and Ledger framed the realistic threat as an external measurement implant (shunt + fast ADC) hidden in a malicious USB cable or power bank delivered by supply-chain or evil-maid substitution; Ledger rated it non-critical and 'highly impractical', found no evidence such an implant existed, but acknowledged the circuitry would fit in hollow cable/power-bank sections.
findings.evidence: LSB-006 (2019-08-07) verbatim: 'The power consumption of each row-based display cycle depends on the number of illuminated pixels, allowing a partial recovery of display contents'; 'a direct correlation was found between the number of illuminated pixels on each row of the display and the total power consumption'; 'the voltage potential over a so-called shunt resistor in the USB cable towards the target device ... which is possible without any modifications to the hardware wallet itself'; 'Although deemed highly impractical ... it would fit directly in hollow sections of a malicious USB cable or a power bank'; 'No evidence was found of the existence of such a hardware implant'. Trezor blog (validated via NVD reference + MITRE CVE-2019-14353, Medium returned 403): 'requires unique components that are typically not present in USB circuitry ... sample the voltage drop over a shunt resistor ... fit directly inside hollow sections of a malicious USB cable ... supply chain attack ... evil maid attack'. NVD scores CVE-2019-14353 AV:P (physical). Reitter's status summary lists all nine CVEs, shows traces distinguishing BIP-39 word pairs (weird/cram, weird/zoo, century/cram), and notes bounties paid by SatoshiLabs and Ledger. Only word-pair discrimination was demonstrated, not full end-to-end seed extraction; the practicality caveat is Ledger's self-assessment.

findings.claim: The leak recurred on the newer, non-SSD1306 panel in the Ledger Nano X and Nano S Plus: an anonymous researcher reported (and Ledger Donjon confirmed, 2023-01-19) a strong correlation between per-row lit-pixel count and total device power during PIN entry, exploitable by spying on power via a malicious USB cable or power bank. Ledger's earlier physical-noise countermeasure (randomised contrast/supply/oscillator parameters plus colour inversion, shipped Q4 2019 for SSD1306) was found insufficient on the new panel; Ledger stated that 'no amount of physical noise could efficiently hide the dependency between the power consumption and the displayed data', forcing a UI-level fix.
findings.evidence: Ledger Donjon post (01/19/2023) verbatim: 'The vulnerability is based on the fact that the power consumption of the screen strongly depends on the displayed content ... a strong correlation was found between the number of illuminated pixels on each row of the display ... and the total power consumption'; 'on the new screen model, this countermeasure was observed to be insufficient: no amount of physical noise could efficiently hide the dependency'; 'We would like to thank the anonymous researcher'. The 2019 oled-vuln post already conceded 'these vulnerabilities can never be fully solved'. Minor internal inconsistency in Ledger's own history: the 2019 post lists the Nano X among SSD1306 devices while the 2023 post calls the Nano X / S Plus panel a 'new model'. The claim 8 vote was 2-1 only because it credited Donjon with the discovery; the physics and recurrence are undisputed.

findings.claim: Every shipped vendor mitigation for the OLED power side channel is a firmware/rendering-level 'make the leakage secret-independent' fix, not a hardware change: (a) Trezor One 1.8.2 (Aug 2019) adds a computed number of white decoy pixels per row so each row of the seed-word band has a constant lit-pixel count (floor = 30 px, the BIP-39 wordlist maximum; 35 for the 21st-word layout), extended in 1.8.3 to the PIN matrix (oledSCAInside, grow-from-centre), explicitly called a 'first round'; (b) Ledger Nano X / S Plus (announced 2023-01-19) replaced digit rendering with a moving dash under a static digit row so the lit-pixel count per row is independent of the selected digit; (c) Coldcard 2.1.2 (Aug 2019) draws random-length masking lines along the right-hand side of every seed-word row, with Coinkite stating that without a working PoC it 'is not possible to conclusively prove that this plugs the leak'. Trezor's approach removes the leak by construction (constant count); Coldcard's adds noise, which Ledger later judged ineffective in principle on its own panel.
findings.evidence: Trezor: verified in the attached /home/nicola/repos/trezor-firmware checkout at tag legacy/v1.8.2 — legacy/oled.c:455 oledSCA(y1,y2,width) 'Mitigate SCA on lines y1-y2 by setting at least width pixels white'; call sites legacy/firmware/layout2.c:836 ('30 is the maximum pixels used for a pixel row in the BIP39 word abstract'), recovery.c:469 (35), pinmatrix.c:51; commit 3f00c61a2f (2019-08-28) 'make sca pixels for pin matrix grow from the inside' adds oledSCAInside (oled.c:479), shipped in 1.8.3 (tag 2019-09-04); CHANGELOG.md:331 '## 1.8.2 [August 2019] ... OLED display security improvements'; blog: 'This first round of mitigation is part of the latest stable firmware 1.8.2. We are looking into additional countermeasures'. Ledger: 'The straightforward way is to make the number of illuminated pixels in each row constant ... the user simply needs to move the dash line under it and validate'. Coldcard: blog verbatim 'we've added masking noise along the right hand side of the screen ... Since we don't have a working proof-of-concept, it's not possible to conclusively prove that this plugs the leak'; firmware repo at tag 2019-08-02T1804-v2.1.2 shared/display.py:181 mark_sensitive draws per-row lines of length max(2, rng()%32) ending at WIDTH-4; still present in current master (display.py:201, ux_mk4.py:510). MITRE CVE-2019-14356 cites the noise-troll post. Note: masking code already existed at v2.1.1; v2.1.2 is the version Coinkite publicly attributed.

findings.claim: A 2024 peer-reviewed power side-channel attack (Park, Kim, Kim, Hong, Korea University, IEEE Access vol. 12) recovers a hardware wallet's master seed by targeting the SHA-2 compression inside HMAC during seed derivation rather than the asymmetric signing primitive, with no profiling phase and — per the authors — no valid credentials; however, on stock Trezor firmware the leaky HMAC window is PIN-gated, so this should be weighted as a laboratory result, not a demonstrated stock-product PIN bypass.
findings.evidence: Abstract (DOAJ API, Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar agree): 'Cloning Hardware Wallet Without Valid Credentials Through Side-Channel Analysis of Hash Function', pp. 132677–132688, CC BY-NC-ND; 'leverages power traces obtained during the processing of the Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code (HMAC), or more precisely, the Secure Hash Algorithm 2 (SHA-2) inside the HMAC'; 'our attack can be conducted without a profiling phase'; prior work characterised as requiring 'sophisticated environmental controls or detailed knowledge of target device' or 'valid credentials'. Full text unreachable (IEEE Xplore HTTP 418/403), so target device, trace counts and exact derivation step (PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 vs BIP-32 HMAC-SHA512) are unverified. In the attached trezor-firmware, mnemonic_to_seed is only called from legacy/firmware/config.c config_getSeed after config_getMnemonic (storage unlocked ⇒ PIN) and from config_compute_u2froot at setup; core/src/apps/common/mnemonic.py:52 also runs post-unlock. Relevance to PQSigner: the analogous PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 → HMAC-SHA512 derivation runs in S-world after dual-SE unlock, so the window is likewise PIN-gated but the SHA-2 power leakage class is directly applicable to the PQ KDF and C10 hashing.

findings.claim: The academic basis for 'current-sense fingerprinting' / 'self-test for added bus load' is the body of work detecting hardware tampering (Trojans/implants, counterfeit parts, physical manipulation) through tamper-induced changes in a board's power delivery network (PDN) impedance and signal-trace characteristics, surveyed in ACM TODAES 31(2) (online 2026-01-28). The literature splits into golden-reference methods (compare against a known-good OEM board or self-enrolled fingerprint) and golden-free methods (design-file-simulated golden signature, e.g. WPI 'Parasitic Circus' arXiv 2403.12252; fleet clustering/hypothesis testing, e.g. NYU IEEE Micro 2023). For wallets this distinction is decisive: a supply-chain implant inserted before first boot is included in any self-enrolled first-boot baseline and so defeats it, whereas design-derived or fleet-distribution references are not defeated by pre-enrolment insertion. The survey does not mention hardware wallets, SPI/display buses, or in-firmware self-tests, and does not establish that a low-cost wallet MCU can detect a high-impedance passive SPI tap.
findings.evidence: Crossref-registered abstract (dl.acm.org returned 403): 'A key emphasis of this survey is on hardware security techniques that leverage alterations in electrical characteristics induced by tampering. These include changes in power delivery network (PDN), signal trace, and other low-level electrical pathways. Such variations often serve as sensitive indicators of physical intrusions or modifications'; 'We examine both golden-reference-based and golden-free detection approaches, highlighting their operational principles, design tradeoffs, and applicability in different threat scenarios'; scope 'hardware Trojans, counterfeit components, and physical manipulations' from ICs to PCBAs to complete end-user devices. Authors Sun, Ding, Zhu (WashU), Jin (USTC), Zou (SJTU); Zhu and Jin are the PDNPulse authors. Corroborating golden-free motivation: NYU 'state-of-the-art hardware Trojan detection methods require a golden PCB system/model'; Parasitic Circus replaces the physical golden sample with a simulated one. The first-boot inference is the claimant's, not the survey's, and holds only for self-enrolled baselines. Verifier's one search surfaced only corroborating work (ChipletQuake arXiv 2504.19418, NSF 2338069, US patents on PDN tamper detectors).

findings.claim: PDNPulse (Zhu, Shan, Sullivan, Guo, Jin, Zhang; IEEE TIFS 2023, arXiv 2204.02482) is the strongest verified board-level implant detector but is an offline golden-reference bench technique, not an on-device runtime self-test: boards are measured unpowered with a Keysight E5063A VNA over 300 kHz–3 GHz (2-port shunt-through, SMA adapters soldered to the PDN) and classified against OEM golden boards by a modified Fréchet distance with KNN/threshold. On a custom 2-layer SoC board (n=4, Trojans toggled by jumpers) it detected an always-on 1 Ω power-SCA sampling resistor (low-frequency impedance 0.2 Ω → 1.2 Ω) and an ATtiny85 triggerable Trojan at 100% TPR / 0% FPR, and the authors extrapolate a ~0.02 Ω detection floor for series-inserted resistors from ±10% PCB fabrication tolerance (arithmetic, not measured). Self-declared limitations: cannot distinguish manufacturing flaws from malicious modification, fails with insufficient/wrong ports or voltage domains, is explicitly 'not designed as a tamper-evident technology', and excludes transient/non-persistent modifications — so it cannot catch a field-installed implant removed before inspection and does not replace tamper evidence.
findings.evidence: Verbatim from the PDF text (pdftotext, scratchpad pdnpulse/paper.txt): 'We utilize the Keysight E5063A VNA and take the 300KHz-3GHz as the band of interest'; 'all measurements are performed off-line without powering the boards'; 'genuine boards (i.e., the golden model) can be those supplied directly from the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) ... If the deviation of the PDN impedance profiles exceeds the recorded tolerance for the golden model, we can reasonably regard a board under test as untrusted'; Sec. IV-C 'Frechet Distance-based Anomaly Detection Algorithms'; Sec. V-A1 'The always-on Trojan is a malicious sampling resistor enabling power side-channel analysis attacks and the value of the resistor is set to be the typical 1Ω ... we can effectively detect all three Trojans, and achieves 100% TPR and 0% FPR ... impedance below 10MHz raises from 0.2Ω to 1.2Ω ... with ±10% PCB fabrication tolerance, we can detect malicious resistors larger than 0.02Ω'; Sec. VI/VII 'it can be difficult to distinguish between manufacturing flaws and malicious modifications'; 'could suffer detection failures when insufficient or inappropriate ports/voltage domains are measured'; 'PDNPulse is not designed as a tamper-evident technology and attacks that can be undone, or are not persistent physical modifications, are outside its scope'; 'Our method is not designed to pin point the root causes or malicious intent'. Their Arduino Due board M3 was anomalous for unexplained reasons. The paper files run-time monitoring under other authors' side-channel work (Sec. VIII); its own future work is port-selection simulation. The companion on-chip/runtime claims from eprint 2022/946 (ring-oscillator PDN sensing detecting an FTDI on TX/RX, 22.42 mΩ at 169.85 MHz; Wasserstein threshold on Arty S7) were REFUTED in verification (votes 1-2, 1-2, 0-3) and must not be cited as establishing on-device added-bus-load detection.

caveats: (1) Framing mismatch: no verified source supports the research question's 'October 2026' or 'CryptoBilis' labels; the only confirmed implant source is Grand's hardwear.io USA 2026 deck (Santa Clara, slides revised 2026-05-29) about a device first reported on Reddit in August 2025. The deck says 'new iterations have already been spotted' without detail; a separate citation is needed for any later variant. (2) Coverage gaps: nothing survived verification about what Trezor (Safe 3/5), Coldcard (Mk4/Q), Keystone, Cypherock, NGRAVE or BitBox actually ship against display-bus implants — no claims about mechanical no-cavity design, tamper-evident packaging, SE-driven displays (Ledger Secure Screen efficacy), or no-display backup flows (Cypherock's Shamir cards, NGRAVE's QR/paper flow) were confirmed or refuted; their absence here is absence of verified evidence, not evidence of absence. (3) The on-device/runtime PDN sensing claims (eprint 2022/946) were all refuted or unverifiable in this run, so there is currently no cited support for a firmware self-test detecting a passive SPI tap on a cheap MCU; the only verified detector is a VNA bench method. (4) Several load-bearing primary pages were unreachable (Trezor Medium blog 403, dl.acm.org 403, IEEE Xplore 418), so those claims were validated via NVD/MITRE references, Crossref abstracts, and the local trezor-firmware and Coldcard source trees rather than the original pages; verifiers' WebSearch budgets were exhausted on most items, so contradiction searches were shallow. (5) Ledger's response is reported secondhand through the researcher's slide; a first-party Ledger statement to press may exist. (6) Vendor 'highly impractical' assessments (2019) are self-interested and predate the 2026 implant; the 2019 shunt-in-cable scenario and the 2025/26 SPI-tap implant are distinct channels (power rail vs data bus) and must not be conflated — a pixel-count-equalising mitigation does nothing against a bus sniffer, which reads the actual glyph bytes. (7) The 2024 HMAC/SHA-2 SCA paper's target device, trace count and success rate are unknown (abstract only); its 'without credentials' property likely rests on a lab target since stock Trezor gates the derivation behind PIN. (8) Time-sensitivity: Ledger's blog/LSB record was checked through 2026-10-07/Aug 2026; a hardening announcement after that would change finding 3.
openQuestions: Can a wallet MCU detect a high-impedance passive SPI/display-bus tap at runtime (bus-line capacitance/rise-time measurement, I/O-rail current signature, loopback timing) with a false-alarm rate acceptable in the field, given that the only peer-reviewed on-chip impedance-sensing claims (eprint 2022/946) failed verification and PDNPulse requires an unpowered board and a VNA?

Which shipped designs actually remove the display from the seed-backup and PIN path (Cypherock X1 Shamir cards, NGRAVE Graphene/ZERO, Keystone/BitBox SD-card or QR flows, Ledger Recover) and do any of them keep secret-bearing data off every sniffable inter-chip bus — i.e. is 'never render the seed' a deployable mitigation for a dual-SE architecture like PQSigner's, and what does the FSBL/measured-boot story look like without a trusted boot-time display?

What does a golden-free electrical fingerprint look like for a wallet: can a design-file-derived or fleet-distribution PDN/SPI-line signature (Parasitic Circus / NYU style) be checked at factory RDP-0 verification time or during the first field boot such that a pre-enrolment supply-chain implant does not poison the baseline, and how does it interact with the ±10% fabrication tolerance floor?

Is the implant class escalating (Grand's 'new iterations already spotted'): have any variants moved from passive display-bus capture to active bus or button injection, and has Ledger or any other vendor published a first-party post-mortem, mechanical redesign, or tamper-evident enclosure in response after 2026-10-07?
